articles.title: The Firm That Decided The Whole World Was Its Market
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Which Biglaw firm was founded in 1949 by a Chicago lawyer who’d grown up poor in New Mexico — and, by some accounts, hopped freight trains to get to law school — on an idea the profession found faintly ridiculous: that a single law firm could span the globe, serving clients in every major commercial capital becoming the first truly multinational law firm in the world?

Hint: It opened its first foreign office in Caracas, Venezuela, in the 1950s, and was decades later led by a woman who went on to run the International Monetary Fund and the European Central Bank.

See the answer on the next page.

The post The Firm That Decided The Whole World Was Its Market appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Beware Of FUBARS
articles.content:
Have you noticed, or perhaps it’s just me, that FUBARS tend to breed? If there is one FUBAR, more emerge. What’s the difference between a SNAFU and a FUBAR? Degrees of idiocy.
So how is this for a FUBAR? Tennessee tries to execute a female death row inmate, Christa Pike, by lethal injection. After repeated failed attempts to kill her by that method (problems finding a vein and other mishaps by nonmedical staff at the prison), she lived and was rushed to the hospital. The hospital treated her and released her back to prison. Does anyone beside me see the FUBAR here? If the stated intent was to kill her, then why take her to the hospital? Is this an oxymoron, with the emphasis on moron?
I’m not sure whether this is a FUBAR or just a run of the mill SNAFU. We expect that judges should behave in a judicial manner, and I shouldn’t have to explain what that means. Google it if unclear. A Florida judge has been publicly reprimanded for stating in open court that he was thinking about shooting lawyers appearing before him. That judge had also described the attorneys as “Keystone cops” and the “Apple Dumpling Gang.” Again, if you don’t know the references, Google them. The judge has apologized (duh) and recused himself from handling matters involving the appearing lawyers. He has also acknowledged that he needs to chill when there are contentious matters before him. Aren’t most matters contentious? If not, they wouldn’t be litigated.
Some folks may consider this merely a SNAFU, but I think this is definitely a FUBAR. In the “What were they thinking?” aka the Chutzpah Department, disbarred California lawyer John Eastman is making a return engagement to the ATL news by signing on to help Penn law professor Amy Wax beat back her own tale of woe. Wait, what? The disbarred Eastman is going to represent Wax? How can he? The California Bar pulled his ticket to ride. He can’t even appear pro hac vice.
And then there’s Katie Zacharia, 47’s new press secretary. who claims that she is a lawyer. She graduated from law school in 2011. However, any bar passage anywhere? Jurisdiction, admission date and bar number, please. Turns out she failed the bar and is still referring to herself as a lawyer. Snafu or FUBAR?
What’s in a name? In “Romeo and Juliet,” Shakespeare wrote that a “rose by any other name would smell as sweet.” That may be true for roses, but what about for what our profession chooses to call, “ahem,” hallucinations?
Naturally AI is top of mind these days everywhere, as is that delightful term “AI slop.” And of course, there are always hallucinations, which can and do get lawyers in trouble with the bar. I don’t think that these should be called “hallucinatons.” That is really too polite a term. What you find in a brief or letter or any other documents citing nonexistent authority is not a hallucination, but, at the very least, a misrepresentation. A lie by any other term is still a lie. With the possibility of bar discipline, not to mention bench slaps of varying degrees and consequences, should we use the term “FUBAR” instead?
And as if we needed yet another cringeworthy lawyer stunt that is definitely FUBAR material, what about Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt, the former Missouri attorney general, who tried to gotcha former Special Counsel Jack Smith in a Judiciary Committee hearing last week?. Schmitt attempted to portray Smith as a liar/perjurer when Schmitt asked Smith a question that puzzled Smith, about whether he had attended a Hawks game in Atlanta on a certain date. But Schmitt had confused the Atlanta Hawks with the Iowa Hawkeyes. Whoops! Now who looks stupid? Leave it to a woman senator, Amy Klobuchar, to clean up the mess.
Schmitt also called Smith a “total dirtbag.” Who is the dirtbag here? Charming language for anyone to use or be described as. And who says that there’s no civility left among lawyers? No wonder that we are held in such low regard, as we should be, given these kinds of antics. Call it what you will: SNAFU or FUBAR. There’s probably a better expression for this kind of behavior. Suggestions welcomed.
Jill Switzer has been an active member of the State Bar of California for over 40 years. She remembers practicing law in a kinder, gentler time. She’s had a diverse legal career, including stints as a deputy district attorney, a solo practice, and several senior in-house gigs. She now mediates full-time, which gives her the opportunity to see dinosaurs, millennials, and those in-between interact — it’s not always civil. You can reach her by email at oldladylawyer@gmail.com.
The post Beware Of FUBARS appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Partners Want AI To Help Them Find New Business, But Most Are Running It On Data They Can’t Use, Introhive Survey Finds
articles.content:
Partners at law and accounting firms say the one thing they most want from business-development technology is help finding new business in relationships their firms already have. But 78% say the relationship data at their firms is hard to act on, and most of those using AI for business development are using general-purpose chatbots that cannot see that data at all.
Those are among the findings of a survey of 123 partners released today by Introhive, the relationship intelligence company that captures and maps firm relationships from email and calendar data.
The report, AI and Business Development in Law and Accounting Firms, was conducted for Introhive by the strategy firm Thinktiv. It drew 42 responses from legal services, 42 from accounting and 39 from other professional services.
“Partners are being asked to grow the book with AI, and most of those using it are doing so with a chatbot that has no access to their firm’s relationship data,” Introhive CEO Lee Blakemore said in a statement accompanying the report.
In an exclusive interview yesterday with LawSites, I asked Blakemore what most surprised him about the findings. He said the results left him with “mixed emotions.”
“There’s this perception that firms and people are far more progressed than they really are,” he said. “I see all of the energy and all the momentum and all the rush to deploy AI, and it seems like it’s almost at a frantic pace right now.
“I’m not surprised to see that although there’s been a lot of money invested and a lot of progress on deployments, there’s still a lot of work to be done in regards to actually adding value and changing the way work has been done. I guess I was surprised that I wasn’t surprised.”
Great Ambitions for AI and BD
The report categorizes firms into four stages of business development maturity, from basic data hygiene (Stage 1) and relationship visibility (Stage 2) to structured BD programs (Stage 3) and AI-driven BD (Stage 4).
Of the partners who responded to the survey, 57% said their firms sit at Stage 1 or 2. Yet 84% expect to reach Stage 3 or 4 within 18 to 24 months, and the number expecting to run AI-driven BD grows from eight respondents to 40.
Asked whether that timeline is realistic, Blakemore said he would “never want to bet against the largest law firms in the world.” The challenge, however, is that the target keeps moving.
“It’s kind of like that old black-and-white photograph of the land grab in Oklahoma, all the carts waiting for the gun to go off,” he said. “Everybody’s racing right now as fast as they possibly can. And as soon as they get to where they wanted to get to, there’s going to be something ahead of them.
“Two years from now, when people have gotten to that 84%, I think they’re going to be talking about where they still need to get to.”
Among partners already using AI for business development, 68% rely only on general-purpose tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini. They rate their satisfaction with those tools at 6.7 out of 10. Just 22% say their firm has a fully developed and implemented AI strategy, even though 51% say strategy is the biggest driver of AI return on investment.
What Partners Say They Want
Asked to name the single BD capability they most want done well each week, 47% chose surfacing new business opportunities, well ahead of who-knows-whom mapping (24%) and automated data capture (17%).
Asked what they would most value from combining information across the firm, they ranked cross-sell opportunities (54%), alerts on at-risk relationships (49%) and relationship mapping (46%) at the top. Credit attribution ranked last, at 15%.
Their biggest sources of friction, according to the report, are knowing where to focus BD time (50%), making time for BD (45%) and identifying cross-sell opportunities (43%). Partners rate the overall difficulty of business development at 3.4 out of 5.
Blakemore said the contrast between what partners want and what they can do with their data was the finding that struck him most.
“They know the information’s there, but they don’t know what to do with it,” he said. “Law partners specifically understand that there is an opportunity within the relationship data they have, their contacts, their network. They want to take action there, but they’re struggling to take action.”
A New Interface for An Old Problem
I asked Blakemore how much of that struggle is a software problem and how much is endemic to professionals who simply do not like entering data. He conceded that CRM adoption at law firms has been “negligible,” and said the reason is structural.
“In order to get the effectiveness you wanted out of the CRM, you needed people to go spend time in it, and history has shown the likelihood of that happening was pretty low,” he said. “In professional services, the ability to dictate the behavior of your end-user professionals is somewhat limited. You’re just not going to dictate that to law partners.”
But AI can change that equation, he said, by becoming “the new user interface,” one that prompts a lawyer to act rather than asking the lawyer to log into a separate system.
“If you expect the attorney to pull their head out of whatever they’re doing and go log in someplace else to write some email to somebody they hadn’t talked to in 90 days, they’re not going to do it,” he said.
“But now, in their day-to-day workflow, they can be prompted: ‘You haven’t talked to Bob in 35 days. Would you like to send an email? Here’s a script.’ You can do all of that on your treadmill, in your earbuds. That’s what people want.”
Of course, that only works if the underlying data is accurate, he said.
“The threshold for quality in CRM was, you’re going to send out a Christmas card list and if you got some bounce-backs, it was okay,” he said. “That can’t be the case anymore. If it’s all automated, it has to be accurate. It has to work.”
Measuring Return
According to the survey, 63% of firms have no revenue-linked way to measure BD return on investment. Instead, 28% track intermediate metrics such as introductions and meetings, 22% track usage and logins, and 13% have no formal measurement. Only 15% can track revenue with strong attribution.
The most convincing proof of BD value, partners in the survey said, would be cross-sell and expansion revenue (44%) and pipeline generated or deals influenced (35%).
I asked Blakemore how Introhive proves its own ROI to customers when most firms cannot connect BD activity to revenue. He acknowledged it is not easy.
“It starts with a person’s disposition toward the topic,” he said. “If you are skeptical that having quality data is going to lead to more business for you as a lawyer, then whatever business case I provide, you’re going to be able to poke holes in it. You’ll say, ‘I would have known that anyway,’ or ‘Your data didn’t produce the business, my relationship produced the business.'”
What does work, he said, is the “if I had only known” dilemma.
“If I had only known this, I would have contacted Bob a lot sooner than I did, and I probably would have won that business,” he said. “That’s how we tend to make the case. But I’m not going to say it’s a slam dunk. It’s in the eye of the beholder.”
MCP and ‘Agnostic’ Access to Data
The report includes a section that discusses Introhive’s MCP server and why it matters to BD. The server lets customers use assistants such as Claude, Harvey, ChatGPT and Copilot to query the firm’s relationship data, subject to each user’s existing permissions and the firm’s governance policies.
While Blakemore was candid that the report’s discussion of MCP is partly self-serving, he believes it was essential for Introhive to provide MCP access to its customers.
“Our clients are large, global, billion-dollar-plus organizations,” he said. “We’re not going to dictate much to them in regards to what platform they should use, and we’re probably not going to win much shelf space on their desktop.
“So, for us, we need to be the data provider of high-quality, accurate, secure data and provide it wherever you happen to work, whatever platform you choose. MCP is just a vehicle that allows us to do that.”
He said that Introhive has taken the same agnostic approach to AI vendors as it has to CRM vendors, noting that AI purchasing inside firms is often run by IT or innovation groups rather than the marketing and BD teams.
A Complex Environment
Blakemore said the survey results should be read against a broader set of forces reshaping both the legal and accounting professions.
While AI is one of those forces, he also pointed to pressure on traditional business models and – in accounting especially but now increasingly in legal – the arrival of private equity ownership, which he said is “starting to change the culture” by putting top-down pressure on partners to generate pipeline and revenue.
“You have the AI trend, you have the AI pressure on the business models, and then you have two of these industries undertaking a level of transformation as it relates to outside investment,” he said. “You’ve got three dimensions happening at once, which makes for a very complex environment.”
Add to that what he called a “keep up with the Joneses” dynamic driven by competitors’ press releases, and partners who are now being asked to take on BD responsibilities they once left to marketing staff.
“All those factors create a lot of anxiety,” he said.
I asked him what law firms should take away from the report.
“Deploying AI without having the quality data to make it actionable, you’re kind of throwing money away. But also, fundamentally, this isn’t about AI. This is about getting people to have a behavioral change.”
“You can deploy all the technology,” he said, “but if you don’t make it usable, if you don’t get the data right, if you don’t do the change management, you’ll be sitting there having deployed all these tools and you still won’t have moved the needle on the thing that mattered. That’s a tale as old as technology itself.”

articles.title: Finally, A Way To Measure AI ROI: Be Careful What You Ask For
articles.content:
In case anyone wasn’t listening, Legora, the legal AI provider, and Laurel, a work intelligence platform provider, recently announced a “partnership.” A partnership that reportedly has two main parts. It will offer what sounds like a fairly standard timekeeping tool. But it holds out the promise of an intriguing future tool that raises some possibilities.
And for users, the latter prompts some that suggest they may need to be careful what they ask for. (As a bit of an aside, I always wonder what these tech vendor partnerships really mean and what obligations come with them. Especially when the key announcement hinges on something the partners plan to do together.)
Automated Time Entry (Yawn)
The first part is an automated time entry program that turns every task a lawyer performs in Legora into a time entry. Reportedly, it will provide the client, the matter, and what was done for subsequent review.
That part of the partnership isn’t all that remarkable. Other vendors and providers have offered similar time entry programs for some time. Presumably the pitch is that those tools may not work as well with Legora. But Legora itself announced a similar integration with Intapp Time not long ago.
And I can just hear a Legora/Laurel representative going, “But ours is so much better.” Maybe it is. Maybe it’s the greatest thing to happen to timekeeping since the invention of the six-minute increment. I can’t really speak to that but do know that other products are out there.
The Bigger Piece
The more interesting part of the announcement is something considerably more than an automated time entry program. And it raises some questions that may make firms a little uncomfortable.
According to the Legora press release, “Laurel and Legora will jointly develop ways to measure how Legora is used, and the value that AI-powered legal work brings to law firms.”
The Legora press release goes on to say that the goal is to give law firm leaders “a clearer view of how their lawyers work, how much they rely on Legora, what work is done on Legora, and the value that Legora delivers.”
Laurel is even more blunt in its release: “Every firm adopting legal AI eventually asks the same thing. They know what it costs, but what are they getting back?… Laurel and Legora will keep working together beyond the timesheet, developing ways to measure how AI-powered legal work is used and what it is worth to a firm…”
What Legora and Laurel are promising is to give law firm management the ability to determine the ROI on their purchase of Legora. The ROI for most AI platforms has indeed proven elusive, except for administrative and nonbillable work where AI replaces human work. I can only assume those trying to determine Legora’s ROI have faced the same difficulty. Hence the effort.
I get it. Law firms spend a lot of money on an AI tool. So it might be nice to be able to say, “Here is the value that we got for it” to those partners who may be scratching their heads and saying, “What the hell did we spend so much money on?”
ROI. To Who?
But calculating the ROI, which is assumed to be the time saved by AI, presents some interesting issues for firms. As I have written, for firms billing by the hour, the ROI of AI platforms that replace substantive legal work really accrues to the client. Or should.
The whole premise is that the AI will do work, perhaps much of which had previously been done by paralegals or associates. That’s billable work, and for firms that use the billable hour model, that’s hardly a return on investment. To the contrary, it’s a loss. Try explaining at the next partners’ meeting that you’ve just spent a ton of money on something that reduces their year-end shares. And be ready for the question: is it too late to back out of this deal? Time saved is not necessarily money earned.
The Legora/Laurel partnership presumably will measure the time saved by Legora AI. Which is easily convertible to dollars. The question then becomes: What does a law firm do with those dollars? Does it pass them on to the client? And what if clients want to see those numbers?
As in, “We want to see the savings your tools came up with so we can determine whether our bills reflect that reduction.” What happens when the tool for justifying the technology investment becomes negotiating leverage for the client? Once you start measuring AI’s value, the next question is who gets to keep it.
There Is Value. For a Different Model
The real value in knowing these numbers, however, is to use them under a different sort of billing system. Like flat fee or outcome-based systems. There, knowing the value of what the AI tools have provided becomes critical. Either in calculating the fee or in running a cost-benefit analysis that compares the savings to the outcome.
That’s a good thing. Especially if it pushes firms to adopt those models and the clients accept them. (Don’t be too hasty to conclude all clients will want alternative billing. They’re not dumb. If they believe AI is dramatically reducing the time required to perform legal work, some may develop a sudden intense affection for hourly billing.)
A Tricky Calculation?
I also wonder how the savings are going to be calculated. It’s a bit tricky and prone to generalization. Suppose it’s determined that it would have taken an associate 10 hours to draft a brief, but using Legora, it only took 6 minutes. That, in and of itself, would reflect a tremendous savings. At $400 an hour, that’s almost $4,000. (Although I’m not sure what the associate would be doing for the other 9 hours 54 minutes.)
It’s easy to say that the time not spent by the associate times their rate is the savings and the ROI. But what about the time spent revising the brief? Checking the citations? (You damn well better check Legora’s or any other vendor’s AI citations if you want to avoid embarrassment, sanctions, or even worse.)
Will that time be netted against the time the AI saved? How will the complexity of the matter factor into the calculation? Should it? It’s a complicated matrix, and it will be interesting to see what Legora and Laurel come up with and how firms treat it.
Another Fly in the Ointment
Another fly in the ointment. By determining the ROI and the savings from AI, will firms unknowingly encourage additional overreliance on AI? In other words, will a partner tell an associate to simply use Legora to do everything, instead of doing the part of the work a human should do? This could particularly be an issue when the work is billed on a flat fee basis where the firm keeps part or all of the savings.
Or perhaps even more problematic. Will clients demand that AI tools be used once they see the savings, to the exclusion or reduction of the needed human work? The reasonable human inquiry that the attorney, by signing a pleading, certifies took place.
Here’s a chilling thought for firm management: What if the numbers show that clients should be paying less? What if they expose inefficiencies management would rather not acknowledge? Few places to run. Few places to hide.
So don’t think that this is nirvana.
That Does Not Necessarily Make It A Bad Thing
That’s not to say calculating the ROI is a bad thing. And it’s not to say Legora and Laurel aren’t providing a helpful tool. (Of course, both have a self-interest in demonstrating the dollar savings.) The questions, though, as with most technologies, primarily fall to the users of these tools.
There are real savings out there from the use of AI. And firm management needs to know what those savings are. They need to know to be transparent with their partners. Particularly in a ponderous consensus-driven decision-making model like most law firms use. They need to know the numbers to be transparent with their clients. And to have any hope of competing on price and quality in the post-AI world.
So what Legora and Laurel are doing is a good thing. But law firm management might want to be damn sure it understands what it’s asking for. You never know, it might just get it. And then what will it do?
Stephen Embry is a lawyer, speaker, blogger, and writer. He publishes TechLaw Crossroads, a blog devoted to the examination of the tension between technology, the law, and the practice of law.

What Legora and Laurel are promising is to give law firm management the ability to determine the ROI on their purchase of Legora. The ROI for most AI platforms has indeed proven elusive, except for administrative and nonbillable work where AI replaces human work. I can only assume those trying to determine Legora’s ROI have faced the same difficulty. Hence the effort.

I get it. Law firms spend a lot of money on an AI tool. So it might be nice to be able to say, “Here is the value that we got for it” to those partners who may be scratching their heads and saying, “What the hell did we spend so much money on?” 

ROI. To Who?

But calculating the ROI, which is assumed to be the time saved by AI, presents some interesting issues for firms. As I have written, for firms billing by the hour, the ROI of AI platforms that replace substantive legal work really accrues to the client. Or should. 

The whole premise is that the AI will do work, perhaps much of which had previously been done by paralegals or associates. That’s billable work, and for firms that use the billable hour model, that’s hardly a return on investment. To the contrary, it’s a loss. Try explaining at the next partners’ meeting that you’ve just spent a ton of money on something that reduces their year-end  shares. And be ready for the question: is it too late to back out of this deal? Time saved is not necessarily money earned.

The Legora/Laurel partnership presumably will measure the time saved by Legora AI. Which is easily convertible to dollars. The question then becomes: What does a law firm do with those dollars? Does it pass them on to the client? And what if clients want to see those numbers? 

As in, “We want to see the savings your tools came up with so we can determine whether our bills reflect that reduction.” What happens when the tool for justifying the technology investment becomes negotiating leverage for the client? Once you start measuring AI’s value, the next question is who gets to keep it.

There Is Value. For a Different Model

The real value in knowing these numbers, however, is to use them under a different sort of billing system. Like flat fee or outcome-based systems. There, knowing the value of what the AI tools have provided becomes critical. Either in calculating the fee or in running a cost-benefit analysis that compares the savings to the outcome. 

That’s a good thing. Especially if it pushes firms to adopt those models and the clients accept them. (Don’t be too hasty to conclude all clients will want alternative billing. They’re not dumb. If they believe AI is dramatically reducing the time required to perform legal work, some may develop a sudden intense affection for hourly billing.) 

A Tricky Calculation?

I also wonder how the savings are going to be calculated. It’s a bit tricky and prone to generalization. Suppose it’s determined that it would have taken an associate 10 hours to draft a brief, but using Legora, it only took 6 minutes. That, in and of itself, would reflect a tremendous savings. At $400 an hour, that’s almost $4,000. (Although I’m not sure what the associate would be doing for the other 9 hours 54 minutes.) 

It’s easy to say that the time not spent by the associate times their rate is the savings and the ROI. But what about the time spent revising the brief? Checking the citations? (You damn well better check Legora’s or any other vendor’s AI citations if you want to avoid embarrassment, sanctions, or even worse.) 

Will that time be netted against the time the AI saved? How will the complexity of the matter factor into the calculation? Should it? It’s a complicated matrix, and it will be interesting to see what Legora and Laurel come up with and how firms treat it. 

Another Fly in the Ointment

Another fly in the ointment. By determining the ROI and the savings from AI, will firms unknowingly encourage additional overreliance on AI? In other words, will a partner tell an associate to simply use Legora to do everything, instead of doing the part of the work a human should do? This could particularly be an issue when the work is billed on a flat fee basis where the firm keeps part or all of the savings. 

Or perhaps even more problematic. Will clients demand that AI tools be used once they see the savings, to the exclusion or reduction of the needed human work? The reasonable human inquiry that the attorney, by signing a pleading, certifies took place. 

Here’s a chilling thought for firm management: What if the numbers show that clients should be paying less? What if they expose inefficiencies management would rather not acknowledge? Few places to run. Few places to hide.

So don’t think that this is nirvana. 

That Does Not Necessarily Make It A Bad Thing

That’s not to say calculating the ROI is a bad thing. And it’s not to say Legora and Laurel aren’t providing a helpful tool. (Of course, both have a self-interest in demonstrating the dollar savings.) The questions, though, as with most technologies, primarily fall to the users of these tools.

There are real savings out there from the use of AI. And firm management needs to know what those savings are. They need to know to be transparent with their partners. Particularly in a ponderous consensus-driven decision-making model like most law firms use. They need to know the numbers to be transparent with their clients. And to have any hope of competing on price and quality in the post-AI world. 

So what Legora and Laurel are doing is a good thing. But law firm management might want to be damn sure it understands what it’s asking for. You never know, it might just get it. And then what will it do?
